articles.title: Nepal floods: IFRC delivers safe water and health care to affected communities
articles.description: Country: Nepal Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies Kathmandu/Kuala Lumpur/Geneva, 8 September 2026 - The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) warns that many families remain cut off from essential services and humanitarian assistance in flood-affected areas of Nepal. Widespread damage to roads, bridges and communication networks is hampering access to some communities, creating significant challenges for the humanitarian response and leaving people exposed to continuing monsoon rains. The IFRC and Nepal Red Cross Society (NRCS) are providing emergency shelter, health care, clean water and sanitation, and mental health and psychosocial support. In Nuwakot, for example, the IFRC, together with NRCS, has installed water tanks and a water pump, helping restore access to safe drinking water for around 2,000 people. Water is also being trucked to affected communities while teams continue to assess longer-term solutions to repair and rehabilitate damaged water systems. With much of the existing water network destroyed, emergency water supply remains a lifeline for families affected by the floods. In the same area, with IFRC support, the NRCS has deployed a mobile primary health care clinic that can reach 100 patients per day, helping to bring essential health services closer to affected communities and address gaps in basic services. "Before the flash flood, it took around three hours to reach Dhunche in Rasuwa from Nuwakot. Today, the journey can take nine hours or more along narrow and dangerous routes," said David Fisher, IFRC Head of Delegation for Nepal. "Every delay means families wait longer for the support they urgently need. We are especially concerned about people not yet reached who remain exposed to harsh conditions. At the same time, the needs of those we have reached in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and other affected areas remain extensive and will require sustained support." Road damage is making access to medical care difficult. With monsoon rains continuing, there are concerns that further damage to access routes could leave communities even more isolated. “We continue our work as fast as we can; we cannot leave anyone behind. While emergency assistance remains our immediate priority, recovery will take time. Together with the Nepal Red Cross Society, we remain committed to supporting communities as they rebuild their lives, livelihoods, and resilience,” Fisher said. Humanitarian needs continue to be significant and will continue well beyond the immediate emergency phase. The IFRC is calling on donors and partners to support its Emergency Appeal to help ensure that people affected by the floods receive the assistance they urgently need and are supported to rebuild their lives in the months ahead. For more information or to set up an interview contact: [email protected] In Kathmandu: Fleur Verwer, +31 6 31752821 In Kuala Lumpur: Lili Chin, +60 16 234 0872 In Geneva: Tommaso Della Longa, +41 79 708 4367 Paolo Cravero, +41 79 894 8396

articles.title: Solomon Islands: Tuma Volo’s story of survival and recovery after Cyclone Maila | IFRC
articles.description: Country: Solomon Islands Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies Text and photos by Ben Bilua, Solomon Islands Red Cross volunteer. The morning of July 22, 2026, began with a mission of hope. Two vehicles carrying Solomon Islands Red Cross volunteers rolled out across Gizo Island, heading deep into communities still recovering from the devastating impact of Category 5 Tropical Cyclone Maila. Their mission was simple but significant: deliver relief supplies to families whose lives had been turned upside down by one of the most powerful storms to strike Western Province in recent memory. Among the many stories of hardship and resilience uncovered that day was that of 60-year-old Tuma Volo of Sitokava village. As the convoy pulled into the village, volunteers noticed an elderly woman sitting quietly by the roadside. Curious about the unusual activity, she watched as they unloaded relief supplies for affected households. When volunteers explained their purpose, Volo did not hesitate to share her story. A night of terror "A mango tree fell on our house and we are trying to fix it at the moment," she said. For Volo and her family, Cyclone Maila was not just another storm. It was a terrifying experience that nearly ended in tragedy. She recalls the night in April the cyclone struck with frightening clarity. "My husband and I were sleeping with our grandchildren when the tree fell on our house," she said. The sound of the crashing tree jolted everyone awake, plunging the household into confusion and fear as powerful winds battered their home under cover of darkness. "Luckily, it landed only inches away from where my husband, me and my grandchildren were sleeping. We hurried to the kitchen. We arranged a small space, put down our mat and stayed there until morning," she said. Throughout the night, the family listened to the howling winds outside, waiting anxiously for daylight. It was only after sunrise that they fully understood how close they had come to disaster. "In the morning, we realised the mango tree had landed only a few metres from the centre of the house," Volo explained. The tree had damaged a significant portion of the structure, leaving the family exposed to the elements. With limited resources, her husband made temporary repairs using sheets of corrugated iron to prevent further damage. "My husband put some roofing iron over the damaged area and we moved back into the house, but it still needs more repairs before it can be properly fixed," she said. For an elderly couple living largely on their own while caring for grandchildren, rebuilding has not been easy. "My husband and I are too old. We are living alone with our grandchildren. Our children lived on the other island working," Volo said. The emotion in her voice reveals that the cyclone left more than damaged homes in its wake — the psychological scars remain fresh, particularly among the children. "The wind was very strong. My grandchildren were frightened and we remained indoors for the whole week," the 60-year-old said. She describes the experience as unlike anything she had witnessed in her lifetime. "It was scary. I thought it was the end of the world because I have never experienced such strong winds in my entire life," she said. They hadn't been forgotten Volo's words echo the experiences of thousands across Western Province who endured Cyclone Maila's destructive force. Homes were damaged, food gardens destroyed and livelihoods disrupted as communities struggled to recover from the aftermath. For families like hers, assistance from humanitarian organisations has provided a much-needed lifeline. After hearing her story, Red Cross volunteers gave her a tarpaulin to cover the damaged section of her home while permanent repairs are arranged, and ran sessions with families on how to install and use tarpaulins for shelter. For Volo, the tarpaulin represented more than shelter, it was immediate protection from further weather exposure, and a sign that her family had not been forgotten. The encounter in Sitokava village served as a reminder that behind every assessment report and relief distribution are real people facing real challenges. For Solomon Islands Red Cross volunteer Maekera Melo, helping people in times of disaster is more than just work — it is a calling that gives purpose to his life. Whenever disaster strikes, Melo puts aside his personal commitments to answer the call for help, believing that serving others during their most difficult moments is both a privilege and a blessing. "Helping others who are affected by disaster is something that I give my utmost effort. This voluntary work with Red Cross gives meaning to my life. It also justifies why we as human beings must learn to help others," he said. Melo was among the volunteers who responded immediately after Cyclone Maila struck. Together with fellow first responders, he travelled to some of the worst-affected areas, including east to north Vella La Vella, North Ranongga, Simbo and the Shortland Islands. The mission was not easy. Volunteers faced rough seas and strong winds as they moved between islands to deliver assistance, relying on vetted hired vessels when the water grew too choppy for smaller boats. Despite the challenges, Melo remained committed to the task, driven by a desire to bring hope and comfort to families struggling in the aftermath of the disaster. His dedication reflects the spirit of volunteerism that continues to inspire communities across the Solomon Islands — local people stepping forward in extraordinary times to help those in need. About Cyclone Maila Category 5 Tropical Cyclone Maila was one of the most destructive weather events to affect Solomon Islands in recent years, bringing destructive winds, torrential rainfall, storm surges and widespread flooding across Solomon Islands and Papua New Guinea. Thousands of people were affected across Western and Choiseul Provinces, with homes, schools, churches, clinics and community infrastructure damaged or destroyed, and food gardens, crops and livelihoods suffering significant losses. Following the cyclone, the Solomon Islands Red Cross moved quickly to deliver food, shelter kits, tarpaulins, hygiene kits, water and medical assistance to affected communities, reaching more than a thousand families across Western Province. The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) supported the Solomon Islands Red Cross throughout the response, releasing funding from its Disaster Response Emergency Fund (IFRC-DREF) to enable an immediate scale-up of relief operations. IFRC support also went toward training Red Cross volunteers in shelter assistance, helping ensure families received safe, dignified and timely help such as the tarpaulin that reached Volo's home. Throughout, the Solomon Islands Red Cross coordinated closely with the Solomon Islands Government, provincial governments, churches and other humanitarian partners, ensuring the response was complementary and avoided duplication. -- As climate-driven storms grow more frequent and severe across the Pacific, preparedness remains one of the most powerful tools communities have. articles.title: Indonesia wildfire haze threatens children across SE Asia and closes schools
articles.description: Countries: Indonesia, Philippines Source: Save the Children JAKARTA, 7 Sept 2026 – Haze from wildfires across Indonesia, intensified by El Niño-driven dry conditions, is spreading across Southeast Asia, threatening children's health and forcing more than 1.4 million students into remote learning, Save the Children said. Intense wildfires in Indonesia’s Kalimantan and Sumatra regions have burned thousands of hectares of land including on Borneo, the world’s third largest island and home to one of its most biodiverse tropical rainforests. The fires have released what the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service described as "massive" carbon emissions.[1] More than 1.4 million students in affected areas in Indonesia have moved to online or remote learning while the air quality remains dangerous. About 12,800 schools across Borneo and Sumatra remain closed shut, according to government data. Save the Children has distributed 8,500 masks to children and families across three districts in Kalimantan. The charity is also raising awareness about how children and families can protect themselves from the harmful effects of haze through posters and leaflets. Capital cities in Southeast Asia were ranked among the top 10 cities with the worst air pollution globally on Monday. The haze had spread as far as the Philippines more than 800 kms (497 miles) away. [2] While parts of Southeast Asia experience an annual slash-and-burn season, often linked to agricultural expansion including some illegal fire practices, Indonesia is facing especially severe conditions this year. A powerful El Niño event is driving prolonged dry weather and heightened wildfire risk that is expected to continue into early 2027 [3]. While air pollution affects everyone, children are among the most vulnerable because their bodies, organs and immune systems are still not fully matured and children absorb more pollutants than adults as they tend to breathe faster, said Save the Children. Exacerbating the situation, the volcano Anak Krakatau is erupting in Indonesia’s Sunda Strait, spewing ash across Western Indonesia and affecting communities, schools, fishing activities, and international air travel. [4] Save the Children is raising awareness among communities in Indonesia affected by the most recent eruption including through “How-To” infographics aimed at helping to keep children safe during a volcanic eruption. [5] Arshad Malik, Regional Director Asia, Save the Children, said: "The Earth, our home, is on fire, and children including here in Asia are being left to bear the consequences. Wildfire smoke in Indonesia has now spread further afield and is exposing children to harmful air pollution that can impair lung development and respiratory health before their lungs have fully matured while their education and wellbeing also suffer. “This is not just a health or an environmental crisis, it is a child rights crisis. Governments and corporations must act now to tackle the root causes of these wildfires, prevent future wildfires and protect children from the devastating impacts of exposure to polluted air.” Save the Children has been working in Indonesia since 1976, responding to major humanitarian disasters like the 2004 tsunami and the 2018 Sulawesi earthquake. Save the Children works in over 100 countries tackling climate change across everything we do and putting children at the heart of climate action. References: [1] https://atmosphere.copernicus.eu/copernicus-indonesias-seasonal-fires-intensify-boreal-wildfire-smoke-impacts-northern-hemisphere [2] https://www.iqair.com/gb/world-air-quality-ranking [3] https://wmo.int/news/media-centre/el-nino-set-become-very-strong-raising-risks-of-extreme-weather-2027 [4] Volcanic Eruption Map spotlight: https://www.iqair.com/newsroom/volcanic-eruption-map-spotlight-anak-krakatau-indonesia [5] https://www.instagram.com/p/Dc72RIIk4QN/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&stkn=MzRlODBiNWFlZA==
